newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmaker concerned about Social Security plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmaker concerned about Social Security plan.

text.p: Senator Phil Gramm on Wednesday raised concerns about a proposal to allow the U.S. government to invest Social Security funds in the private financial markets rather than allowing individuals to direct such investments.
"I can assure you that's not going to happen on my watch because I am very concerned about it," the Texas Republican who chairs Senate Banking Committee's Securities Subcommittee said at a hearing.

His comments follow proposals unveiled in January by a special advisory panel that was asked to come up with strategies to ensure the future financial health of Social Security, which provides benefits to 44 million Americans.

Some members on the Advisory Council on Social Security suggested allowing the government, not individuals, to invest up to 40 percent of the Social Security trust funds in the private financial markets.
Gramm is not alone in his concerns about such a move.

"I think the mother of all bad ideas would be to allow the federal government to invest Social Security funds in the stock market. I can't imagine anything worse than the director of human services deciding what company we should buy stock in," said Senator Lauch Faircloth.

Gramm, while noting dramatic funding reforms for Social Security will be needed over the next 25 years, said more research needs to be done before any changes involving stock market investing are put in place.
Currently, Social Security funds can be invested only in special issue Treasury securities, which provide a low-risk but lower rate of return than other investments.

One other proposal of the 13-member advisory group would turn Social Security into a two-tiered system under which all retirees would received a flat benefit when they retire. But individuals would also be allowed set up persoanl savings accounts, in which up to five percent of their annual Social Security payroll tax could be invested elsewhere.
"I believe that this is a good idea whose time has come, but obviously there are a lot of problems that we've got to look at," Gramm said.
